title: Air pollution and health effects: A study of medical visits among children in Santiago, Chile.
ehr_evidence: Data on morbidity due to respiratory diseases among children under 15 years of age have been collected from a group of public primary health clinics.
summary: Time-series study examining associations between daily air pollution (PM10, ozone) and clinic visit counts for respiratory symptoms among children in Santiago, Chile.
key_findings: PM10 was significantly associated with lower respiratory symptoms (LRS) in both children under 2 and children aged 3-15.
PM10 was associated with upper respiratory symptoms (URS) only in the older cohort.
Ozone was associated with both URS and LRS in the older cohort.
For children under 2, a 50-μg/m3 increase in PM10 was associated with a 4-12% increase in LRS.
For children aged 3-15, a 50-μg/m3 increase in PM10 was associated with a 3-9% increase in LRS, and a 50 ppb increase in ozone was associated with a 5% increase.
No significant association was found between PM10 or ozone and nonrespiratory symptoms.
Ozone was not significantly associated with respiratory symptoms in children under 2.
population: children under 15 years old in Santiago, Chile (<2 years and 3-15 years)
limitations: aggregate daily counts rather than individual patient records
clinic visits reflect subjective parental decisions and may be influenced by clinic capacity and operating hours
data only represent lower and moderate income populations
lack of data on sulfur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide
potential for discouraged demand bias at high pollution levels
